title: Streaming protocol + serialization: latency vs $/request sandbox
body:
Purpose:
A short sandbox comparing end-to-end client->Redwood runtime latency and per-request cost impact for different streaming protocols and serialization formats. This is a working doc for decisions on default SDK transport (HTTP/1.1 JSON, HTTP/2 gRPC+proto, HTTP/2 with compact-binary framing) and recommended compression knobs for low-latency interactive products.

High-level takeaway (tentative):
- For low-token, high-imbalance interactive workloads (short user prompt + streamed tokens): HTTP/2 gRPC + tiny-protobuf framing yields best p50 latency and stable p90 at modest CPU cost.
- For large bulk responses or embedding batches, framed binary + gzip at client side reduces egress bytes and $/request at the expense of small p50 increase; prefer for non-interactive bulk endpoints.
- JSON-over-HTTP remains simplest but pays 1.6x median latency and 1.8x bytes in our microbench compared to proto-framed streaming for short-turn chat.

Bench goals and constraints:
- Measure real wallclock latencies from an instrumented client sitting in same AWS region as Redwood backend (us-west-2) to isolate serialization + runtime + network serialization overhead.
- Focus on three workload patterns: interactive short-turn streaming, long-context single-shot generation (4–8k tokens), and embedding batch (64 inputs).
- Capture p50/p90/p99 latencies, request size (client->server), response size (server->client), CPU usage proxy (client-side observe), and per-request egress bytes which feed into $/GB pricing.

Environment (hardware/software):
- Client machine: c6i.large (Linux), 2 vCPU, 4GB, us-west-2.
- Redwood runtime: prod-like pool on p4d-equivalent (benchmark cluster), stable model variant: open-llama-13b-quant (deterministic tokenization for repeatability).
- Network: VPC peered test path, measured median RTT 6ms.
- SDKs: python-async SDK (branch bench/stream-proto), NodeJS streaming client (same branch) used for cross-check.
- Serialization formats: JSON (text), Protobuf (tiny message: {request_id, prompt, stream:bool, compression_hint}), CBOR (binary), MessagePack, and a compact custom framing (length-prefixed protobuf + optional gzip).
- Protocols: HTTP/1.1 (POST), HTTP/2 over TLS (gRPC), HTTP/2 with bidirectional streaming (raw framed).
- Compression: gzip client-side for large payloads; no compression for tiny messages in interactive path unless explicitly tested.

Workload details:
1) Interactive short-turn streaming (S): 10k requests over 10 minutes, prompt size median 120 bytes, expected response stream 6–40 tokens (avg 22 tokens).
2) Long single-shot (L): 500 requests, prompt + context ~6k tokens, response ~512 tokens.
3) Embedding batch (E): 200 requests, batch of 64 short inputs (~250 bytes each), single response with 64 vectors returned.

Primary metrics (table):
- p50,p90,p99 latency: end-to-end from first client write to first token received (for streaming) or final byte (for non-stream).
- request_bytes_in, response_bytes_out, percent_cpu_client, bytes_per_request (for $ calc)

Representative results (median of 3 runs each) — interactive S workload:
Format | Protocol | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | req_bytes(B) | resp_first_token_bytes(B) | resp_total_bytes(B)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
JSON   | HTTP/1.1  | 78      | 210     | 540     | 480          | 720                       | 2,400
Proto  | gRPC H2   | 42      | 120     | 320     | 360          | 420                       | 1,220
CBOR   | H2 framed | 48      | 135     | 360     | 380          | 440                       | 1,330
MPACK  | H2 framed | 45      | 128     | 350     | 370          | 430                       | 1,300
Proto+Gzip | gRPC H2 | 46    | 140     | 380     | 210          | 420                       | 1,050

Notes: p50 measured to first token; response_total includes subsequent chunks over streaming connection. JSON shows tail p99 blowups due to header + repeated text encoding overhead and longer payload frames; proto reduces framing overhead and CPU-bound serialization time. Proto+gzip reduces request bytes significantly (client->server) but the compression step adds ~4ms on client CPU in these small messages.

Long single-shot L workload (final-byte latency):
Format | Protocol | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | req_bytes(B) | resp_total_bytes(B)
---------------------------------------------------------------------
JSON   | HTTP/1.1  | 360     | 1,120   | 2,560   | 420,000      | 1,200,000
Proto  | gRPC H2   | 320     | 980     | 2,200   | 400,000      | 880,000
Proto+Gzip | gRPC H2 | 370   | 1,050   | 2,300   | 60,000       | 210,000
CBOR   | H2 framed | 330     | 1,050   | 2,300   | 390,000      | 840,000

Notes: For large payloads, gzip shows the biggest $/request win because network egress is the dominant cost. However, proto+gzip pushes p50 slightly higher due to client compression time and server decompress cost (but server decompression happens prior to model execute, pipelined in runtime). In production we could use streaming decompression pipelines to hide some of this.

Embedding batch E workload (bytes and $):
Format | Protocol | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | total_resp_B | client_req_B | bytes_per_vector(B)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
JSON   | HTTP/1.1  | 420     | 1,400   | 6,200,000    | 1,600,000     | 97
Proto  | gRPC H2   | 380     | 1,120   | 4,050,000    | 1,250,000     | 63
Proto+Gzip | gRPC H2 | 460   | 1,300   | 980,000      | 210,000       | 15
MPACK  | H2 framed | 390     | 1,150   | 3,900,000    | 1,200,000     | 61

$/request rough calc (back-of-envelope):
- Assumptions: egress $0.09/GB, request ingress free; compute and model cost excluded (focus strictly on network-economics).
- For S (interactive) use resp_total_bytes as egress, convert to GB then * $0.09
Example: proto streaming S avg resp_total_bytes 1,220 B => 0.00000114 GB => $0.000000104 per request (negligible)
- For L (long single-shot) proto+gzip resp_total_bytes 210,000 B => 0.000195 GB => $0.0000176 per request (tiny but multiplied by high volume it's material)
- For E (embedding) proto+gzip total_resp_B 980,000 B => 0.00091 GB => $0.000082 per request (per 64-vector batch)

ASCII mini-visual: normalized p50 (interactive S) lower is better (proto baseline=1.0)
proto  | ####### (1.0)
mpack  | ######## (1.07)
cbor   | ######### (1.14)
json   | ################ (1.86)
proto+gz | ####### (1.09)

CPU and client-side impact summary:
- Proto before compression: serialization negligible (sub-ms) on modern client CPU.
- gzip on client: for small messages adds ~3–6ms overhead depending on CPU; worthwhile only when request/response > ~64KB.
- JSON encoding for streaming increments (per-chunk) amplifies CPU cost when tokens are emitted frequently; observed CPU throttle on constrained clients leads to extra jitter.

Operational considerations:
- Observability: streaming protocols require token-level tracing to attribute where latency occurs (network vs runtime vs serialization). Add end-to-end hooks in SDK to sample first-byte and subsequent-chunk times.
- Backwards compatibility: keep HTTP/1.1 JSON as fallback for legacy integrations but mark it as higher-latency path.
- SDK defaults: choose gRPC H2 + tiny-proto framing for interactive SDKs, add a transparent gzip switch for batch endpoints where response payloads > 128KB.
- Edge cases: some mobile clients have poor H2 stacks; provide an HTTP/1.1 chunked+msgpack fallback with server-side adaptors.

Risks and unresolved questions:
- Model-side CPU on decompress path: our bench used a prod-like runtime with pipelined decompression, but real customer workloads could see spikes. Need dedicated bench measuring server decompression concurrency and impact on tail latency.
- TLS handshake cost for short-lived connections — in these runs we used pooled connections. Need to re-check cold connection scenarios for mobile flows.
- CDN or WAN cross-region egress cost variance: network price assumptions need validation for enterprise customers with negotiated egress discounts.

Recommendations (next steps):
1) Draft SDK change: default to gRPC H2 streaming with protobuf framing for interactive clients; add config toggle for "batch_compression_threshold_bytes" default 128KB. (PR: bench/stream-proto #72)
2) Run server-side decompression concurrency sweep to quantify p99 effect under load (open ticket PROT-241).
3) Add token-level instrumentation in SDKs to capture serialization + chunk emission delay.
4) Prototype a small mobile-friendly fallback (HTTP/1.1 + msgpack chunking) and test p50/p90 on low-end Android (arm64) devices.

Appendix: Quick bench notes and commands used:
- python bench client: bench/stream-proto/run_stream_bench.py --protocol grpc --format proto --streams 10000 --region us-west-2
- sample artifacts stored: s3://redwood-bench/stream-proto/2027-11-15/
- raw logs: https://logs.redwood.internal/streams/stream-proto/2027-11-15 (requires internal access)

Open questions we should poll in next sync:
- threshold for enabling gzip by default for Hosted API? 64KB or 128KB?
- do we expose streaming protocol selection to the customer or keep it internal mapping based on client capability?
- for Dedicated customers in air-gapped setups, what's the preferred default, given some infra stacks don't support HTTP/2 well?

Notes-to-self: preserve these raw numbers in case product requests a one-pager; re-run against new runtime kernels when p4d->p5-class infra arrives (likely Q1 2028).

End of sandbox draft.
